thread.title_full: 'Fabric of America' Exhibit Examines Fashion's Evolution and History - NewsBreak

author: Erica Banas
title: 'Fabric of America' Exhibit Examines Fashion's Evolution and History - NewsBreak
text:
By Erica Banas ,
8 hours ago On a sunny afternoon in June, I drive to the Henry Ford Museum of American Innovation — a place I love to explore but admittedly haven’t visited in a few years — for a private tour of an important new exhibit: Fabric of America: Our Fashions, Textiles, and Technologies .
My tour guide is Marc Greuther, the museum’s vice president of historical resources and chief curator. Branding and identity specialist Jeff Newsom joins us, along with Meredith Long, former director of collections operations under Greuther.
As we traverse the museum’s immense footprint, I struggle to contain the urge to explore the various exhibits we pass while Greuther explains how the historical resources department takes care of all the collections, from curation and collections management to conservation and registration.
“We get to work with really interesting collections, and we get to grow them and reinterpret them,” Newsom says. “Sometimes, like today, you’ll see what happens when we get to exhibit them in new ways.”
We arrive at our destination. The newly opened exhibit beckons. Immediately in front of us is a delightful mix of tapestries, clothing, furniture, and equipment. The limited-run exhibit (which ends Sept. 13) is part of the museum’s America: 250 Years in the Making commemoration, with items grouped into categories representing five American values: liberty, practicality, inventiveness, abundance, and individualism.
“We were very keen on tapping into the fashion and clothing collections,” Greuther notes. “We’ve acquired an awful lot of material in the last 10 years or so. Fashion and fabric are as good as any subject area or medium as a way of looking at and thinking about American history.”
He leads us to a pristinely preserved patriotic dress made in 1900 that was used in a parade. “What’s startling about this is it’s quite obviously an old dress, but that kind of approach to using the flag as a means of embellishment feels rather modern,” he says.
The exhibit is packed from floor to ceiling, yet it’s thoughtfully arranged for an easy flow.
With more than 700 artifacts, the exhibit makes it easy to linger. I revisit multiple displays, especially the graphic, colorful tapestries that Alexander Girard designed for Herman Miller and a selection of Elizabeth Parke Firestone’s shoes and haute couture dresses — including designs by Dior, Balenciaga, and Yves Saint Laurent. Other items that caught my eye were a wedding dress made from a parachute during World War II (silk had been requisitioned for the war effort), a Nixon campaign dress, and Devo’s Tyvek suits.
Dupont Tyvek “Yellow Suit” or “Radiation Suit” Sold By Club Devo, circa 1980: Famous for its absurdist humor, the new-wave band Devo formed as a critical response to the 1970 Kent State shootings. Founding members Mark Mothersbaugh and Gerald Casale were students and part of the anti-Vietnam War protest where the National Guard opened fire, killing four students. Two were their friends. In 1977, Devo began wearing these modified Tyvek suits, sold as disposable workwear for hazardous waste cleanup. // Photo courtesy of The Henry Ford/EE Berger A grouping of dresses created by American fashion designers is a big draw. The section features pieces from Newsom’s collection, the most recognizable of which is a Donna Karan cold-shoulder dress that Hillary Clinton wore in 1993.
“Jeff’s been very generous with materials he’s collected over the years, so we’ve been building up a nice portfolio,” Greuther says.
To date, Newsom has donated nearly 100 artifacts to the museum. “Some people collect Tupperware,” he jokes.
Fabrics, clothing, machinery, technology, people, places, and moments in time. The Fabric of America exhibit is a kaleidoscopic journey of the essence of America — one of many compelling reasons to visit this treasure of a museum that we are so lucky to have in our own backyard.
The exhibit runs through Sept. 13 at the Henry Ford Museum of American Innovation. It’s free for members or with museum admission.
1 of 3 Displays include a Pullman porter’s uniform, an Indigenous ribbon skirt, and a 1940s Red Cross quilt. // Photo courtesy of The Henry Ford/EE Berger Dorothy Grant’s Raven Bolero and T-Form Dress, 1988 with Shark Hat, 2025: Dorothy Grant (Haida), respected as an elder of the contemporary Indigenous fashion community, has been integrating traditional Haida forms with high fashion since the 1980s. This raven bolero and T-form dress were part of her very first collection — the Feastwear line, released to acclaim in 1989. // Photo courtesy of The Henry Ford/EE Berger Snug Suit, circa 1980: The energy crisis that struck after the 1973 Arab oil boycott and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries’ price increase heightened public awareness that natural resources were not limitless. To reduce energy consumption, Americans began to drive less or switch to vehicles with better gas mileage, turn down thermostats at home, and wear more layers of clothing to keep warm. Heritage Quilters, Inc. created this quilted indoor jumpsuit in response. Its wearer could dial down the heat and don the jumpsuit to stay toasty. // Photo courtesy of The Henry Ford/EE Berger The post appeared first on .
